name: bubblewrap
why: Unprivileged namespace sandboxing is a door into how containers and Flatpak actually isolate processes, though it is Linux-only.

brief.what_it_is: Bubblewrap (bwrap) is a small Linux command-line tool that runs a program inside a sandbox built from kernel namespaces, without needing root. You give it arguments that describe the filesystem view, namespaces, and command to run, and it starts that command in a new, mostly empty mount namespace where the root is a tmpfs invisible to the host. It takes a list of mount and namespace options plus a command, and outputs the sandboxed process's own output and exit status. The README describes it as a low-level building block rather than a finished sandbox with a fixed policy.
brief.why_it_exists: The README argues that tools like docker and systemd-nspawn are built for administrators and orchestrators, and are not safe to give to unprivileged users because access can be turned into a root shell on the host. Bubblewrap is meant to give ordinary users container-style isolation by using unprivileged user namespaces, and to be shared by tools such as Flatpak that need non-root sandboxing.
brief.how_it_works: Bubblewrap creates a new mount namespace whose root is a tmpfs that is invisible from the host, and the user's command-line options then construct the filesystem, process environment, and command inside it. It uses unprivileged user namespaces rather than setuid, and sets PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS to block setuid binaries from escalating. Optional namespaces cover users, IPC, PID (with a small pid1 that reaps children), network (loopback only), and UTS, and seccomp filters can be passed in.

Trimmed illustrative example from the README: starts a bash shell in a sandbox that reuses the host's /usr read-only, sets up /proc and /dev, unshares the PID namespace, and uses a new session. The README calls it incomplete and for illustration only.

brief.install_notes: Most Linux distributions package bubblewrap in their repositories, so installing from the distro is the README's first suggestion. To build from source, the README gives a meson sequence (setup, compile, test, install). The kernel needs support for unprivileged user namespaces, since the setuid mode has been removed. The README does not mention accounts, runtimes, or first-run configuration.
brief.standout: It reaches container-style isolation without setuid by relying on unprivileged user namespaces, and it deliberately stays small so the security-relevant code is easy to audit. Unlike Firejail, it has no desktop-specific features such as PulseAudio filtering; those are left to the calling application.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched README shows no release date, version number, or last-commit date. It does describe current behaviour, such as removing the old setuid mode, and it lists downstream users like Flatpak. I did not check the releases or commit history.
brief.caveats: Linux only, because it depends on Linux namespaces and seccomp. It is not a ready-made sandbox: the protection level is set entirely by the arguments passed in, so a wrong setup gives weak isolation. The README says anything mounted into the sandbox can be used to escalate privileges, for example a D-Bus socket that can run commands through systemd, so xdg-dbus-proxy is suggested for filtering. Without seccomp filtering of TIOCSTI, --new-session is needed to prevent out-of-sandbox command injection (CVE-2017-5226). Some applications with their own sandboxes, such as certain browsers, may fail under these restrictions. The setuid mode is gone, so systems without unprivileged user namespaces are not supported.
quotes: bubblewrap is a tool for constructing sandbox environments. bubblewrap is not a complete, ready-made sandbox with a specific security policy.
bubblewrap works by creating a new, completely empty, mount namespace where the root is on a tmpfs that is invisible from the host, and will be automatically cleaned up when the last process exits.
The name bubblewrap was chosen to convey that this tool runs as the parent of the application (so wraps it in some sense) and creates a protective layer (the sandbox) around it.
